name: Hassan Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I'm not really a technology person, so I'll tell you what I think, not what I'm supposed to think.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a salaried doctor at Oakfield Family Practice, a private group practice on the edge of town owned by three senior partners. I'm in by eight, check the overnight results, then see patients in twelve-minute slots until one. Afternoons are more patients, a couple of home visits to the care home on Linden Road, and paperwork until six. I type my own notes in the old system, my own way, and I don't touch the AI thing the partners bought. I like the care home visits most. What I don't like is that every month the partners talk about margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, now can we stop talking about it. I'd tell the partners to put the money back into a nurse instead of software licences. Most people I know wouldn't care either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my plan still stands, which is to buy into the partnership in three years. But the practice is tight on money already, and the buy-in will cost more than I've saved. So it's not a worry-free picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down, keep my list, and keep saving toward the buy-in, about six hundred a month. My girlfriend Leila and I would keep renting for now. I wouldn't change anything just because of AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly settled, with a bit of a knot about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the knot, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The buy-in. The partners want a big lump sum, and I've got about four months of living costs saved. If the practice has a bad year, the partners might delay the offer, or raise the price. Either way I'm stuck renting longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything about the routine automation touch you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. The partners would use it to answer repeat prescription requests, maybe. I never used it, so I wouldn't miss it.

I'd tell the partners to fund **a nurse**, not software licences.
think: I think my plan to **buy into the partnership** in three years still stands.
The practice is **tight on money**, and the buy-in costs more than I've saved.
do: Keep **my list** and my own way of working.
Save about **six hundred** a month toward the buy-in.
Keep **renting** with my girlfriend Leila for now.
feel: He feels **mostly settled** with a **knot** about money.
S0.quote: If the practice has a bad year, the partners might delay the offer, or raise the price.
fieldNote: His pressure is the **partnership buy-in**, not technology.
He refuses AI by **habit** and sees no reason to start.
A tight practice budget makes even AI Plateau **less than calm**.

steps.text: Keep seeing his list at Oakfield in his usual way
Save six hundred a month toward the partnership buy-in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should go slowly and check everything. I'd say it in the practice meeting, politely, because the partners decide and I don't. Online, I'd say nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the partners would love it. If software writes the letters and books the patients, they need fewer salaried doctors like me, and they don't need to offer anyone a partnership. My plan to buy in could just disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see what the partners actually do in the first six months before moving. If they made the AI note system compulsory, I'd learn it, but only the minimum. And I'd look quietly at the hospital's urgent care centre, where the work is more hands-on, in case Oakfield cut a salaried post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The worst part of it is not the AI, it's that someone else decides what happens to me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think the partners would cut a salaried post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they talk about margins every month. One of them, Dr Grant, already said at the Christmas meal that the future is one doctor per thousand patients plus software. He said it like a joke. Nobody laughed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Leila think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's a pharmacist, and her checking work is right there on the card too. So we'd both be looking over our shoulders. That's what keeps me awake, more than my own job.

I'd raise it **politely** in the practice meeting and say nothing online.
think: I think the partners would need **fewer salaried doctors** like me.
My plan to **buy in** could simply disappear.

Look quietly at the hospital's **urgent care centre** for hands-on work.

fieldNote: He sees **fewer salaried posts** and a lost partnership as the real threat.

steps.text: Wait six months to see if the partners cut salaried posts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless and somebody should slow it down. I'd probably say that to anyone who'd listen, at the gym, at family dinners. I'm not the type to protest, but I'd vote for whoever promised to put brakes on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished at Oakfield within a year or two. Desk medicine, deciding and writing, is exactly what the card says it can do. The partners would keep one or two doctors to sign things off, and they'd be the partners themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to the hospital urgent care centre straight away, because stitching, plastering and examining are hands-on, and robots are three years behind. We'd stop saving for the buy-in and keep the money as cash to live on. Leila and I would put off moving in to a bigger place and probably the engagement too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like the ground went soft under my feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd put off the engagement. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a wedding costs money and I'd want to know I have a job first. My mother would be upset, she's been asking for two years. But I'm not spending ten thousand on a wedding party when I don't know my income next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You never use AI. Would you start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have to, I suppose, to get hired anywhere. But I'd be learning it in a hurry, from behind, which is the worst way. Younger doctors who already use it would get the jobs first.

I'd vote for whoever promised **brakes** on it.
think: I think I'm **finished at Oakfield** within a year or two.
The partners would keep **one or two doctors** to sign things off.

Put off the bigger flat and the **engagement**.

S2.quote: I'm not spending ten thousand on a wedding party when I don't know my income next year.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his post** and sees urgent care as a three-year refuge.
Being **behind on AI** would cost him in hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's be sensible about it. Rules, checks, someone accountable. I'd say that in the practice meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the partnership is gone either way, just later. Five years means I'd watch the partners slowly stop hiring and then stop offering. With robots three years behind, the hands-on side of medicine is where I'd want to be by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the emergency medicine training path in the next year or two, while there are still places. I'd keep saving, but for living costs, not the buy-in. I'd learn the AI system because I'd have to, but slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sharp than the two-year one. More like a long winter coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Emergency medicine is a big change for someone who prefers the familiar. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the familiar is the thing disappearing. I'd rather do one big change on my terms than be pushed around for years. And I'm 27, so I've got the energy now, not at 40.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Leila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd probably move to hospital pharmacy too, where there's more hands-on work with patients on the wards. We'd both be moving toward the hospital beds and away from the desks.

I'd ask in the practice meeting for **rules, checks** and someone accountable.
think: I think the **partnership** is gone either way, just later.
I'd want to be in **hands-on medicine** by 2031.

S3.quote: We'd both be moving toward the hospital beds and away from the desks.
fieldNote: Five years pushes a **resistant** person into one big deliberate change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and things never go to plan. I'd tell people not to panic. That's what I'd tell myself too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd still try for the partnership. Ten years is most of the payback time anyway. I'd be 37 when it hits and 40 before the robots, so I'd have had a good run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on at Oakfield and keep saving for the buy-in. I'd watch what the partners do with the AI and only change if they stopped offering partnerships. Leila and I would get engaged next year like we planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I'd just get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy in. Isn't that buying into a business AI could shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But owning part of the practice that buys the AI beats being the salaried doctor the AI replaces. I hadn't thought of it like that until now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you change course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the partners stopped hiring entirely, or the price of the buy-in went up because the practice expects higher profits from software. Then I'd know which side of the desk I'm on.

I'd tell people **not to panic**, myself included.
think: I think I'd **still try** for the partnership.
Arriving at **37**, I'd have had a good run first.

Watch whether the partners **stop offering** partnerships.

S4.quote: Owning part of the practice that buys the AI beats being the salaried doctor the AI replaces.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd lose my job, my plan and probably my engagement in one year. What would help is a proper path into hands-on medicine, like funded urgent care training, and some notice from employers before they cut posts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the people who own the practices. Salaried doctors like me don't decide anything. The partners who own the practice decide, and we just find out.

headlineQuote: Salaried doctors like me don't decide anything. The partners who own the practice decide, and we just find out.
portrait: Hassan is a **27-year-old** salaried doctor at a private group practice owned by three partners.
He **never uses AI** and prefers his own way of working.
His central plan is to **buy into the partnership**, and AI threatens that more than his skills.
He swings from **uneasy** to alarmed with AGI by 2028, when he'd flee to urgent care.
Given a decade, he realises **ownership** could protect him and keeps his plans.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, losing his job, plan and engagement in one year.
whatWouldHelp: A funded path into **hands-on medicine** like urgent care.
**Notice from employers** before posts are cut.
